sections.title: Policies, Standards, and Procedures
sections.content:
Policies — high-level, authoritative documents defining an org's security commitment (business practices) Standards — more specific than policies; define the methods used to implement technical/procedural requirements (implementation focus) Procedures — detailed, step-by-step instructions describing how to complete specific tasks, aligned to standards Guidelines — flexible recommendations, allow discretion; not mandatory (unlike policies)
COMMON ORGANIZATIONAL POLICIES
Policy | Purpose
AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) | Defines acceptable use of network/computer systems (browsing, content, downloads, sensitive info); requires signed acknowledgment
Information Security Policies | Rules/guidelines for securing information across the org
Business Continuity & COOP (Continuity of Operations Plan) | Keeps critical processes operational during/after a disruption
Disaster Recovery | Steps to recover from catastrophic events (natural disaster, hardware failure, breach)
Incident Response | Process for identifying, investigating, controlling, mitigating, and communicating a security incident
SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) | Governs structured software development from requirements through maintenance
Change Management | Governs how IT/software changes are requested, reviewed, approved, implemented, documented
PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT LIFECYCLE
IAM (Identity and Access Management) spans both IT/security procedures and HR policy, across three phases:
• Recruitment (hiring) — screening candidates, background checks
• Operation (working) — HR communicates policy/training; ongoing security awareness
• Termination or Separation (firing/retiring) — numerous security implications regardless of voluntary/involuntary
Background Checks — verify identity, screen for criminal activity/bankruptcy/risky connections; mandatory for some roles (e.g., federal security clearance); internal or third-party.
Onboarding tasks:
• Secure Transmission of Credentials — initial password/smart card issued securely, protected against rogue admin staff
• Asset Allocation — provisioning devices or approving BYOD
• Training/Policies — scheduling security awareness and role-relevant training
• IAM automation streamlines provisioning, role-based access assignment, and HR system sync
Playbooks — central repository of standardized strategies/tactics; support consistency, knowledge continuity, quality assurance, and are especially critical for incident response/crisis management. Reference frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK, NIST SP 800-61, OSSA.
Offboarding tasks:
• Account Management — disable accounts/privileges; preserve access to company-owned assets (encryption keys, protected files)
• Company Assets — retrieve devices, keys, smart cards, USB media; confirm no retained copies
• Personal Assets — wipe corporate data from employee-owned devices
• Departures of employees with deep security knowledge or shared/generic credential access should trigger immediate credential changes
STANDARDS
Standards define the expected outcome of a task (e.g., a config state or performance baseline). Adoption is driven by regulatory requirements, business-specific needs, risk management strategy, industry practice, and stakeholder expectations.
Industry Standards:
Standard | Focus
ISO/IEC 27001 | ISMS (Information Security Management System) framework
ISO/IEC 27002 | Companion to 27001; detailed control guidance
ISO/IEC 27017 | Extension to 27001 for cloud services
ISO/IEC 27018 | Extension to 27001 for PII in public clouds
NIST SP 800-63 | US digital identity guidelines (password/access control)
PCI DSS | Protects cardholder data environment (CDE)
FIPS | NIST cryptography standards for US federal systems
Internal Standards (implementation-focused, vs. policies' business-practice focus):
• Password Standards — hashing algorithms, salting, secure transmission, reset verification, password managers
• Access Control Standards — access models (RBAC/DAC/MAC), identity verification methods, privilege management, authentication protocols (Kerberos/OAuth/SAML), session management, audit trails
• Physical Security Standards — building security, workstation security, datacenter/server room security, equipment disposal, visitor management
• Encryption Standards — allowable algorithms (AES/ECC), minimum key length, key management (generation/distribution/storage/rotation/revocation)
LEGAL ENVIRONMENT
Governance committees translate legal requirements (regulatory compliance, contractual obligations, disclosure laws, breach liability, privacy, IP, licensing) into operational controls.
Due diligence — legal term meaning responsible persons have not been negligent in their duties; negligence can create criminal/civil liability.
US Laws:
• SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley Act) — mandates risk assessments, internal controls, audit procedures
• Computer Security Act (1987) — requires federal agencies to develop security policies for systems processing confidential info
• FISMA (Federal Information Security Management/Modernization Act, 2002) — governs security of federal agency data
Global/Privacy Law:
Law | Region | Key Point
GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) | EU | Requires informed consent for personal data collection/processing; grants rights to withdraw consent, inspect, amend, erase data
CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act) | California, US | Right to know/delete/opt-out of sale of personal info; applies based on revenue/data-volume thresholds regardless of org location
Data Protection Act 2018 / NIS Regulations 2018 | UK | National cybersecurity/data protection law
PIPEDA | Canada | Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
IT Act 2000 | India | IT industry regulation
Privacy Act 1988 | Australia | National privacy law
Industry-Specific Laws (examples):
Sector | Law(s)
Healthcare | HIPAA (US), GDPR (EU)
Financial Services | GLBA (US), PCI DSS (contractual)
Telecommunications | CALEA (US)
Energy | NERC (US/Canada)
Education & Children | FERPA, CIPA, COPPA (US)
Government | FISMA (US), CJIS (US), GSC (UK)
GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE
Model | Description
Centralized | Single core group/department controls policy, budget, personnel — promotes consistency
Decentralized | Decision-making distributed to departments — allows localized adaptability
Hybrid | Combines both — some processes centralized, others delegated
• Governance Boards — high-level executives + external stakeholders; set strategic objectives, oversee implementation, evaluate program effectiveness
• Governance Committees — subject matter experts/operational leaders; provide analysis and recommendations to the board
Government Entities:
Agency Type | Role
Regulatory Agencies | Establish/enforce sector-specific standards (finance, healthcare, telecom, energy)
Intelligence Agencies | Gather/analyze threat information for national policy
Law Enforcement Agencies | Investigate/prosecute cybercrime
Defense and Military Organizations | National security, defense-related cybersecurity
Data Protection Authorities | Enforce data protection regulations
National Cybersecurity Agencies | Protect critical infrastructure/government networks, coordinate incident response
DATA GOVERNANCE ROLES
Role | Responsibility
Owner | High-ranking employee; ultimately responsible for classification, access decisions, security level
Controller | Identifies purposes/conditions/means of processing personal data (GDPR concept); ensures legal compliance
Processor | Processes data on behalf of the controller (often a CSP); maintains processing records
Custodian | Data steward; handles safe custody/transport/storage, enforces controls set by owner/controller, reports incidents

sections.title: Change Management
sections.content:
Change management — systematic approach to managing all changes to IT infrastructure/products; goal is minimizing risk/disruption while maximizing value. Requires planning, testing, approval, implementation, and rollback plans.
Typical managed changes: software deployments, system updates, patching, hardware replacement/upgrades, network modifications, configuration changes, new product/software integrations, support environment refreshes.
Approval Process:
• RFC (Request for Change) submitted — purpose, scope, potential impact
• Change manager/committee reviews feasibility, risk, policy alignment
• Formal approval by stakeholders (management, IT, impacted departments)
• Documentation/communication tracked throughout
CHANGE MANAGEMENT CONCEPTS
Concept | Description
Impact Analysis | Identifying/assessing implications for users, processes, interconnected systems
Test Results | Evaluation in a test environment before implementation
Backout Plans | Contingency plan to reverse a failed change and restore original state
Maintenance Windows | Predefined recurring time frame for changes, scheduled during low activity
SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) | Written instructions ensuring consistent, effective change implementation
Stakeholders vs. Owners:
• Owners — individuals/groups primarily responsible for implementing a specific change (project managers, team leads); accountable for execution, risk management, communication/training
• Stakeholders — individuals/groups impacted or interested (employees, managers, Change Advisory Board (CAB), customers, vendors, partners)
ALLOW LISTS AND DENY LISTS (CHANGE MANAGEMENT CONTEXT)
• Allow list — approved software/hardware/change types (routine, low-risk) exempt from full CM process; may include pre-authorized approvers
• Deny list — explicitly blocked software/hardware/change types (known issues, high-risk changes requiring full review, unauthorized approvers)
• Caution: hash-based software allow lists can break after patching — patched executables get new hash values and may be blocked, making fully-patched systems unusable. Must be factored into testing plans.
RESTARTS, DEPENDENCIES, AND DOWNTIME
Change Type | Typically Requires Restart
Software Upgrades and Patches | Yes — to apply and activate the update
Configuration Changes | Yes — server/network/database settings
Infrastructure Changes | Yes — switches, routers, firewalls, load balancers
Security Changes | Yes — encryption protocol updates, feature toggles, access control changes
• Scheduled downtime — planned maintenance window; Unscheduled downtime — unavailability from an unplanned outage
• Dependencies — services relying on each other complicate restarts (e.g., restarting a database can affect all dependent apps); dependency mapping is critical to avoid unintended outages and extends both implementation and backout plan timing
Legacy Systems — outdated tech creates compatibility issues with new updates; may require virtualization, emulation, interpreters, or custom "fit-gap" solutions. Often lack documentation and vendor support, compounding risk.
DOCUMENTATION AND VERSION CONTROL
Version control — tracking/controlling changes to documents, code, or data; maintains historical record, ensures only approved changes are live, allows reverting.
Documentation types impacted by change:
Item | Update Trigger
Change Requests | Reflect current status/approvals
Policies and Procedures | Align with new processes/controls
System or Process Documentation | Architecture diagrams, process flows, SOPs, user manuals
Configuration Management Documentation | Tracks configuration item changes (servers, networks, databases)
Training Materials | Presentations, manuals, CBT modules
Incident Response and Recovery Plans | Account for new configurations/dependencies

sections.title: Automation and Orchestration
sections.content:
Automation — software performing repetitive, rule-based tasks (monitoring, patching, baseline maintenance, incident response) to improve efficiency and reduce human error. Orchestration — coordinates/streamlines interactions between automated processes and systems, especially across many tools in complex environments.
AUTOMATION CAPABILITIES
Capability | Description
Provisioning | Creating/modifying/deleting user accounts and access rights (user provisioning); allocating servers/storage/networks (resource provisioning)
Guardrails and Security Groups | Automated policy enforcement; security groups define resource access, managed via automation to reduce excess permissions
Ticketing | Auto-generates tickets from monitoring alerts, routes by criteria, escalates critical/SLA-risk issues
Service Management | Automates enabling/disabling services, modifying access, managing IT resource lifecycle
Continuous Integration and Testing | Automated testing on every code merge; improves quality, speeds development
APIs | Enable system-to-system communication; automation orchestrates these into workflows (e.g., SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response)
BENEFITS AND OPERATOR FATIGUE
Operator fatigue — mental exhaustion from continuous, high-intensity monitoring/alert volume (including false positives); causes decreased alertness, missed critical alerts, slower response, more errors.
Automation/orchestration combat fatigue by:
• Handling routine tasks (vulnerability scanning, patching, monitoring) — a workforce multiplier
• Freeing security personnel for complex/strategic work
• Reducing detection and reaction time via coordinated response (e.g., auto-isolate a subnet, analyze, notify, ticket, and document a threat without human intervention)
• Enforcing standardized baselines automatically, overriding unauthorized endpoint changes
• Supporting staff retention/job satisfaction
IMPORTANT CONSIDERATIONS (CHALLENGES)
• Complexity — requires deep understanding of systems/processes/interdependencies; poorly planned automation adds complexity
• Cost — high initial cost (tooling, integration, training); ongoing maintenance/upgrade costs
• Single Point of Failure — a critical automated system failing can impact multiple areas at once
• Technical Debt — hasty implementation → poorly documented code, brittle integrations, instability over time
• Ongoing Support — requires continuous updates, process review, and staff education to stay effective/secure
INFRASTRUCTURE AUTOMATION BENEFITS
• Consistency/accuracy via standardized configurations
• Time/resource savings, faster deployment, better scalability
• Improved standardization, compliance, and change tracking; controls configuration drift
• Strengthened security/governance via consistent patching and enforced controls

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Implement a governance structure (centralized, decentralized, or hybrid) that best supports the organization's objectives
• Leverage expertise through governance committees to support board-level decision-making
• Establish a comprehensive list of policies, processes, standards, and guidelines, and assign clear data governance roles (owner, controller, processor, custodian)
• Implement change management programs — RFC/approval workflow, impact analysis, testing, backout plans, maintenance windows, and documentation/version control — to maintain control and promote transparency
• Use automation and orchestration tools (provisioning, guardrails, ticketing, SOAR) to improve consistency, reduce response times, combat operator fatigue, and support compliance

concept_cards.hook: A policy that governs employees' use of company equipment and Internet services. ISPs may also apply AUPs to their customers.
Policy mandating work areas free of sensitive documents.
Standards/best practices/guidelines for security risk management.
Creating/monitoring policies/procedures to manage assets and ensure regulatory compliance.

practice_questions.q: Which document states, at a high level, management's intent for how security is handled across the organization?
practice_questions.explanation: Policies set high-level direction; procedures give the steps.

practice_questions.q: Before a firewall rule change is applied in production, who typically approves it?
practice_questions.explanation: Change management routes significant changes to an approval authority such as a CAB.

practice_questions.q: A script automatically creates accounts in five systems when HR adds a new hire. What benefit does this provide?
options: Faster, consistent provisioning with fewer errors
Eliminates the need for access reviews
practice_questions.explanation: Automation makes repetitive tasks consistent and fast.

practice_questions.q: A document says, step by step, how to onboard a new employee's accounts. What is it?
Why does a change request include a backout plan?
options: To document the change after it is done
To list who will pay for the change
To return systems to their prior state if the change fails
To bypass testing for urgent changes
practice_questions.explanation: A backout plan defines how to undo a failed change.

practice_questions.q: A platform runs playbooks that automatically enrich alerts, block IPs and open tickets. What is it?
practice_questions.explanation: Security orchestration, automation and response executes playbooks.

practice_questions.q: A rule that all laptops must use AES-256 encryption is an example of a:
An approved patch will reboot critical servers. When should it normally be applied?
practice_questions.explanation: Maintenance windows reduce the business impact of downtime.

practice_questions.q: An automation script has a bug that disables every user account. Which automation risk does this show?
options: A single error can cause widespread impact
practice_questions.explanation: Automation magnifies mistakes, so scripts need testing.

practice_questions.q: Recommended, but not required, best practices are called:
